cards.title: Compare lattice enthalpies: charge first, then ionic radius

walkthrough.question:
Four ionic solids are listed below. Separating one mole of each into gaseous ions takes a different amount of energy. Which solid needs the most energy, meaning it has the highest lattice enthalpy?
A. MgS
B. MgO
C. CaBr2
D. NaF
walkthrough.key_idea: Highest ion charges win first; then smallest ions give the strongest attraction.
walkthrough.question_type: Compare lattice enthalpies from charge and radius
walkthrough.careful: Compare ions' charge and radius, never atomic radius or electronegativity.
procedure: Write each compound's ions with their charges.
Compare ion charges; larger charges attract more strongly.
Keep only the compounds with the largest charges.
Among those, compare ionic radii using group position.
Choose the smaller ions: centres closer, attraction stronger.
tricks: Spot the 2+/2− compound first; it beats 1+/1− and 2+/1−.
Same charges: smaller ions win. Fails if one shrinks, other grows; check section 16.
Section 16 check: MgO is 3791 kJ mol−1, NaF only 930.
if_lost: What does lattice enthalpy measure: which particles are being pulled apart?
What charge does each ion carry, judging by its group?
Which compounds have the largest charges on both ions?
If charges tie, which anion sits higher in its group?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: pick the one largest value.
4_command_terms.why: An MCQ rewards only the final letter, so no reasoning is written. Get the order of checks right, then stop.
4_command_terms.avoid: Trying to recall all four values; two are not even in section 16.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the compound whose ions attract most strongly, judged from charge and size.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing, for the correct letter. No working is marked.

1_context.short: Lattice enthalpy is a Born-Haber term; compare it by ion properties.
1_context.why: Lattice enthalpy measures separating a solid into gaseous ions, so its size tracks the attraction between those ions. Only ion charge and distance between ions matter here.
1_context.avoid: Reasoning from atomic radii or valence electrons, which examiners reported in trend explanations (12M.2.HL.TZ2.3).
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.5: Born-Haber cycles include lattice enthalpy. Comparing its values is not spelled out there; past papers test it.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show one rule with tidy pairs. This question mixes charge types and sizes, so you must sort by charge before looking at radius.

3_novel_application.short: CaBr2 has three ions, yet 2+/2− pairs still attract more.
3_novel_application.why: Attraction grows with the product of charges and falls with distance. A 2+/2− pair scores four, 2+/1− scores two, 1+/1− scores one. Radius separates similar scores.
3_novel_application.avoid: Choosing by how many ions the formula contains or how heavy the compound looks.
3_novel_application.disguise: Four formulas hide three charge patterns, and the two closest options differ only in their anion.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Rewrite every formula as ions with charges, then rank by charges before looking at any radius.

7_elimination.short: Drop compounds with 1− anions; then S2− loses to smaller O2−.
7_elimination.why: Lower charges mean weaker attraction, so C and D fall. With the same cation and same charges, the larger anion keeps the ions further apart, so A falls.
7_elimination.avoid: Eliminating on electronegativity, a wrong reason examiners flagged in a similar comparison (14M.2.HL.TZ2.8).

definitely_wrong.rule: Both ions are only singly charged, so it cannot beat a 2+/2− pair.
Bromide is only 1− and both ions are large.
Same charges as the other Mg compound, but S2− is larger than O2−.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 16 lists MgO and NaF; it omits MgS and CaBr2.
6_data_booklet.why: The table supports the rule but cannot answer alone. Its series such as MgO to BaO show values falling as ions grow, so you can extend the trend.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting for MgS or CaBr2 values in the table: they are not there.
6_data_booklet.pattern: MgO 3791, CaO 3401, SrO 3223, BaO 3054: values fall down a group. NaF is 930, and MgCl2 is 2540 kJ mol−1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The rule linking charge and radius to lattice enthalpy, and values for MgS and CaBr2, are NOT in section 16. Get charges from group number.

5_time_efficiency.short: Sort by charge, compare one anion pair, done in thirty seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: Charge sorting removes two options at once, leaving one radius comparison. No values or calculation are needed.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Building a Born-Haber cycle or adding terms; nothing here needs a sum.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip exact values, cycle terms and electronegativity. First ionization energy is not a feature that raises lattice enthalpy (08N.1.HL.TZ0.20).

2_markscheme_logic.short: The mark goes to MgO: highest charges and the smaller anion.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Attraction grows with charge and falls with distance between ion centres. Written markschemes credit this distance language for comparisons with the same charges (25M.2.HL.6209.4, 19M.2.HL.TZ1.3).
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Stopping at charge and picking MgS: it ties with MgO on charge, so radius must decide.
trigger_phrases: Letter B alone earns this MCQ mark
Written form: greater distance between ion centres (19M.2.HL.TZ1.3)
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Here the mark stops at the letter. In written answers, the reference must clearly be to ions, not atoms (25M.2.HL.6209.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A and B tie on charge. B wins only because O2− is smaller than S2−, so charge alone stalls at a tie.

walkthrough.answer: B. MgO has 2+ and 2− ions, like MgS, but O2− is smaller than S2−, so its ions are closer and attract most strongly.

1_context.ao: AO2 when ranking compounds in an MCQ; AO3 when explaining a difference in writing.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.5 names lattice enthalpy as a Born-Haber term. Comparing values is not stated in this understanding; the pattern comes from past papers.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach charge and radius as one short rule. Exams mix charge types, ask for full orderings, and demand the word ionic in written reasons.

trigger_phrases: higher charge and smaller radius of the positive ion (08N.1.HL.TZ0.20)
trap_boundaries: A written radius mark needs a clear reference to ions (25M.2.HL.6209.4).
Lower first ionization energy is not a feature that raises lattice enthalpy (08N.1.HL.TZ0.20).
Examiners reported atomic radii, nucleus-to-valence-electron attraction and electronegativity as wrong reasoning (12M.2.HL.TZ2.3, 14M.2.HL.TZ2.8).
IB lattice enthalpies are endothermic and positive, so 'most positive' means largest (13M.1.HL.TZ2.18, 12M.1.HL.TZ1.16).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Examiners reported that most candidates gave the greater charge of Mg compared with Na, but few also added the smaller Mg ion (12M.2.HL.TZ2.3). Name the factor that actually differs: comparing Ca2+ and Mg2+ chlorides comes down to radius (25M.2.HL.6209.4).

disguises: Ordering four compounds instead of choosing one (15M.1.HL.TZ2.17).
'Most positive lattice enthalpy of dissociation' used for largest (13M.1.HL.TZ2.18).
Statements about a positive ion's features, including a first-ionization-energy distractor (08N.1.HL.TZ0.20).
Asking for the lowest value instead of the highest (24M.1.HL.TZ2.18).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Turn every formula into ions with charges. Rank by charge, then by radius, and ignore everything else.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQs give one mark, all or nothing. In the written May 2019 and May 2025 comparisons, one mark goes to the ionic size or ion-centre distance point (19M.2.HL.TZ1.3, 25M.2.HL.6209.4).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip Born-Haber sums, exact values, electronegativity and ionization energies. In a written answer, give only the factor that differs, in ionic terms.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 16 lists lattice enthalpies, so use it to confirm a trend: LiF 1049 down to CsF 759, MgO 3791 down to BaO 3054. The charge-and-radius rule is NOT in section 16, and many compounds such as MgS and CaBr2 are not listed.

rules: A 1+/1− compound cannot beat a 2+/2− compound in these comparisons; section 16 supports this.
With the same charges and one shared ion, the compound with the larger other ion is lower (NaCl above CsCl in 15M.1.HL.TZ2.17).
Any statement that a lower first ionization energy raises lattice enthalpy is wrong (08N.1.HL.TZ0.20).
Exception: if one ion shrinks while the other grows, the rule cannot decide. Section 16 shows CaF2 2651 above MgCl2 2540, so read the table.

evidence.note: Worked question; the markscheme gives B, MgO.
61% showed a good grasp of the factors involved.
Choose the greatest value from MgO, CaO, NaF and KF; answer MgO.
Mixed charge types and anions; answer CaO.
Same pattern worded as most positive; answer MgCl2.
The wording reflects the booklet's endothermic convention.
Increasing order CsCl, NaCl, MgCl2, MgO.
Higher charge and smaller radius count; lower first ionization energy does not.

Part (c)(ii): credit for larger Ca2+ ionic radius or greater distance between ion centres; must clearly say ionic. The question text is cut off in the pack, so this is used only as markscheme wording.
Part (d)(iii): K+ larger than Na+, with smaller attraction from greater distance between ion centres.
Trends often explained through atomic radii or valence electrons; most gave charge, few added size.
The IB programme uses the endothermic definition of lattice enthalpy.
Many wrongly invoked electronegativities when explaining an order of lattice enthalpies.
Very few could explain why calcium bromide has a larger lattice enthalpy than potassium bromide.
Identifying the compound with the lowest lattice energy proved hard.

cards.difficulty_signal: 61% got the worked question right (16N.1.HL.TZ0.19). Written explanations are weaker: very few could explain a calcium and potassium bromide comparison (09M.2.HL.TZ1.6), and May 2012 findings list lattice enthalpy trends as difficult.

cross_links.note: The ionic bonding deck may use the same charge-and-radius idea; check for overlap. This evidence pack covers R1.2 only.
